title: Hawkins, black singers and dancers, and the origin of Chicago jazz
summary: Freeman says he learned from Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith, was awed by Coleman Hawkins's tenor, and calls Chicago jazz a white impression of Oliver and Louis.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Now, to get back to the black business again. I think that I learned more actually from the black dancers and black singers such as Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith than I did from black players, but the strange thing about it all was that I was not influenced by one kind of jazz. For instance, the first time I heard Coleman Hawkins play, I was amazed to hear the powerful authority this man had on the tenor because in those days, tenor was played as an accompanimental instrument. I was supposed to be the first white tenor player to play in a jazz band which simply means they threw out the trombone and put the tenor in. Jimmy McPartland, cornet, Teschemacher, clarinet and myself tenor and that was supposed to have been called later on Chicago Jazz.

But I would like to think that King Oliver and Louis started the so-called Chicago Jazz. Because what we played on those records was our, the white man's impression, of what King Oliver and Louis were doing.
